books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.text:
“...That there is hereby established in the War Department, to continue during the present war of rebellion, and for one year thereafter, a Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands, to which shall be committed, as hereinafter provided, the supervision and management of all abandoned lands, and the control of all subjects relating to refugees and freedmen from rebel States. . . . The Secretary of War may direct such issues of provisions, clothing, and fuel as he may deem needful for the immediate and temporary shelter and supply of destitute and suffering refugees and freedmen, and their wives and children. . . .”

—Freedmen’s Bureau Act, March 3, 1865
stimulus.source_note: Freedmen’s Bureau Act, March 3, 1865 (13 Stat. 507). Public domain. Wording verified against the act text in the Congressional Serial Set (govinfo). Ellipses mark omitted text between passages, quoted in their order in the source.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: By the late 1860s most freedpeople were working as sharecroppers on their former masters’ land, with the landowner supplying seed and land and the worker paying rent in crops. That outcome best shows that

options.text: the Bureau had given every freed family forty acres.
options.misconception: Background: no freed family received forty acres as a rule; Sherman’s order was reversed and Stevens’s land bill died.
Background: a sharecropper owed the landowner for seed and supplies, so debt kept the worker tied to the land.

options.text: the Black Codes had been repealed by 1866.
options.misconception: Background: the Black Codes were still on the books in 1866, and Congress was fighting them.

options.text: freedom without land left most freedpeople dependent on white landowners.

rationales.A: Background: no freed family received forty acres as a rule; Sherman’s order was reversed and Stevens’s land bill died.
rationales.B: Background: a sharecropper owed the landowner for seed and supplies, so debt kept the worker tied to the land.
rationales.C: Background: the Black Codes were still on the books in 1866, and Congress was fighting them.
rationales.D: Freedom gave freedpeople their persons but not the land they worked. With no land of their own, most had to farm someone else’s fields on the owner’s terms, paying rent in crops and sinking into debt.
rationales.general:
1. Sharecropping sounds like a bargain: the owner gives land and seed, the worker gives labor and crops.
2. Background: the worker owned nothing and bought supplies on credit from the landowner.
3. A bad harvest meant debt, and debt meant another year on the same land.
4. So legal freedom without land became economic dependence.
Remember: freedom to work is not the same as freedom to own the ground you work.
